items.prompt: What is a unit test?

options.label: A test that checks how the system behaves when a very large number of users are active at once
A test that checks one small piece of code, such as a function, in isolation
A test that drives the whole application through its user interface like a real user would
A test that a customer runs before accepting the product

rubric: A unit test targets a small unit of code in isolation.
Distractors describe end-to-end, load and acceptance testing.

items.prompt: In an automated test, what is an assertion?

options.label: A setting that skips the test when the machine is too slow to run it
A statement that checks the actual result equals the expected result
A comment above the test that documents what behaviour it covers
A line of setup code that starts the program under test and prepares data

rubric: Assertions compare actual and expected outcomes.
Distractors confuse assertions with setup, comments or skip flags.

items.prompt: What does an integration test check?

options.label: That the code style follows team rules
That one function returns the right value for given inputs
That the server survives a traffic spike
That several components work correctly together

rubric: Integration tests check interaction between components.
Distractors describe unit, linting and load testing.

items.prompt: What is a mock in testing?

options.label: A tool that formats the test report
A copy of the production database used by all tests
A fake object that stands in for a real dependency
A smaller test that runs only the slowest code paths

rubric: A mock replaces a real dependency during a test.
Distractors confuse mocks with timing, tooling or data copies.

items.prompt: What does code coverage measure?

options.label: The number of defects that escaped into production
The speed at which the whole test suite finishes
The share of requirements that the customer approved
The share of code lines run while tests execute

rubric: Coverage is the proportion of code run by tests.
Distractors name unrelated metrics.

items.prompt: Which of these are common levels of automated testing? Select all that apply.

options.label: Syntax highlighting tests
Integration tests
Unit tests
End-to-end tests

rubric: Unit, integration and end-to-end are standard levels.
Syntax highlighting tests is not a testing level.

items.prompt: A new teammate asks you for the name of the common three-part structure of a test: set up the data, run the code, then check the result. You are writing a short guide for them. Which name should you give this structure?

options.label: Plan, Build, Deploy
Init, Loop, Exit
Read, Write, Execute
Arrange, Act, Assert

rubric: Arrange-Act-Assert is the standard test structure.
Distractors are other three-part sequences.

items.prompt: Why do teams usually write many more unit tests than end-to-end tests?

options.label: Unit tests exercise the whole system, so each one covers more behaviour
Unit tests run faster and point to the failing code more precisely
End-to-end tests are slower to run and often fail for reasons unrelated to a bug
End-to-end tests cannot be automated, so teams rely on unit tests instead

rubric: Unit tests are fast and localise failures.
Distractors misstate what each level offers.

items.prompt: Why is a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on unchanged code a problem?

options.label: It shows the code is correct whenever the test passes
It only matters if the test also lowers the coverage number
Nobody can trust its result, so real failures get ignored
It means the test runner is broken and needs reinstalling

rubric: Flaky tests erode trust in results.
Distractors invent benefits.

items.prompt: Why should a unit test for a price calculator avoid calling a real payment service?

options.label: Payment services block outside callers, so code can only reach them through a browser
The real service makes the test slow and dependent on things outside the code
A unit test passes only if it calls real services, so mocks would hide any bugs
Calling a real service would change the calculator's code and make its logic invalid

rubric: Isolation keeps tests fast and deterministic.
Distractors make false claims about code and services.

items.prompt: A function is tested with 100% line coverage. What can you conclude?

options.label: Every line ran, so the function's logic must be correct
Every line ran, so all input combinations have been tried
Every line ran, but the tests may still miss wrong results
Every line ran, so no further tests are needed for edge cases

rubric: Coverage shows execution, not correctness.
Distractors treat coverage as proof of quality.

items.prompt: Which test case is a boundary value test for a function that accepts ages 18 to 65 inclusive?

options.label: Checking that the function name is correct
Checking only the age 40
Checking ten random ages near 40
Checking ages 17, 18, 65 and 66

rubric: Boundary tests probe values at and next to the limits.
Distractors stay in the middle or are irrelevant.

items.prompt: Which statements describe a good unit test? Select all that apply.

options.label: It needs a specific test to run before it
It can run without depending on other tests
It checks a clear expected outcome
It gives the same result every time it runs

rubric: Good tests are repeatable, independent and have clear expectations.
Order dependence makes tests fragile.

items.prompt: A developer fixes a bug where a discount of 0% crashed the checkout. Before closing the ticket, they add a test that applies a 0% discount and expects the normal price. What is the main purpose of this test?

options.label: It proves no other discount can crash
It removes the need for other discount tests
It speeds up checkout for every order
It catches the bug if it returns later

rubric: A regression test guards against a bug reappearing.
Distractors claim unrelated benefits.

items.prompt: Why do unit tests usually run much faster than end-to-end tests?

options.label: They run one small piece of code with no browser, network or database
They run on faster hardware than the machines used for UI tests
They skip assertions so each test finishes as soon as the code runs
They only cover simple code, so there is less logic to execute

rubric: Unit tests isolate a small unit and avoid slow external systems.
Distractors confuse speed with skipped checks or hardware, which are not the cause.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a mock object in an automated test?

options.label: To measure how many lines of the code under test were executed
To stand in for a real dependency and record how it was called
To speed up the code under test by caching its results between runs
To generate random input values so edge cases are found for you

rubric: A mock replaces a dependency and lets the test check interactions.
Other options describe caching, fuzzing and coverage tools.

items.prompt: A test passes on most runs but sometimes fails with no code change. What does this describe?

options.label: A coverage gap, because some branches are not run on every build
A false positive, because the test checks too little of the code
A flaky test, whose result varies because of timing or shared state
A regression, because a recent change to the code has broken existing behavior

rubric: Flaky tests give different results on the same code, often from timing or shared state.
A regression would fail consistently, not intermittently.

items.prompt: A suite reports 100% line coverage. What can you conclude?

options.label: Every branch and condition was exercised with both true and false
Every possible input has been tried, so no bugs can remain in it
Every requirement is met, because each line was checked for output
Every line ran during testing, but the assertions may still be weak

rubric: Line coverage shows execution only, not that behaviour was verified.
Distractors treat coverage as proof of correctness or branch coverage.

items.prompt: A test saves an order through the repository class to a real test database, then reads it back and compares fields. How is this test best classified?

options.label: A smoke test, because it only checks basic function
An end-to-end test, because it checks saved data
An integration test, because it uses a real database
A unit test, because it checks one class

rubric: Using a real database means components are tested together, which is integration.
Testing one class is not enough for a unit test if it uses real external systems.

items.prompt: Which of these are traits of a well-designed unit test? Select all that apply.

options.label: It gives the same result on every run
It fails for one clear reason
It can run alone, in any order
It needs the tests before it to run first
It calls a live web service for its data

rubric: Good unit tests are deterministic, focused and independent.
Order dependence and live services make tests brittle and flaky.

items.prompt: A team's `apply_discount` function has 100% line coverage, and every test passes. A customer still reports a wrong total when the discount is exactly 100%. A developer looks at the tests and sees each one calls the function but only checks that no error is raised. Why did the tests miss the bug?

options.label: The tests were too fast, so they did not reach the discount branch
The coverage tool miscounted lines, so some code was never run
The function needs integration tests, since unit tests cannot find maths bugs
The tests ran the code but never asserted the returned value

rubric: Coverage shows lines ran; without assertions on results, wrong values go unnoticed.
Distractors blame the tool or test type instead of missing assertions.

items.prompt: A function `is_adult(age)` returns `age >= 18`. Which pair of inputs best tests its boundary?

options.label: 18 and 19
17 and 18
10 and 30
0 and 100

rubric: Boundary tests use values just below and at the threshold.
18 and 19 are both adult results, so they miss the switch point.

items.prompt: `discount(price, percent)` should return the price after the percentage is taken off. Which test correctly checks a 25% discount on 200?

options.label: `assert discount(150, 25) == 200`
`assert discount(200, 25) == 150`
`assert discount(200, 25) == 50`
`assert discount(200, 25) > 0`

rubric: 25% off 200 is 150, and the test asserts that exact value.
50 is the discount amount, not the discounted price; `> 0` is too weak.

items.prompt: `send_welcome(user, mailer)` calls `mailer.send(user.email, "Welcome")`. How do you test it without sending real email?

options.label: Call it with a real mailer and check your inbox afterwards
Wrap the call in try/except so that any email error does not fail the test
Pass a fake mailer and assert it received the address and subject
Assert that `send_welcome` returns `None`, since a successful send returns nothing

rubric: Injecting a fake mailer lets you verify the call without side effects.
The other options send real mail, check nothing useful, or hide errors.

items.prompt: A cart test must check that adding an item raises the item count to 1. Which ordering follows Arrange-Act-Assert?

options.label: Create an empty cart, add the item, then assert the count is 1
Add the item, assert the count is 1, then create an empty cart
Assert the count is 1, create a cart, then add the item to it
Create a cart, assert the count is 1, then add the item to it

rubric: Arrange sets up state, Act runs the behaviour, Assert checks the result.
Other orders assert before acting or act before arranging.

items.prompt: `parse("")` should raise `ValueError`. Using pytest, which test checks this correctly?

options.label: `with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse("")`
`try: parse("")` then `except ValueError: pass`
`assert parse("") is ValueError`
`assert parse("") == None`

rubric: `pytest.raises` fails the test if the exception is not raised.
A bare try/except passes even if nothing is raised; the others are wrong or invalid.

items.prompt: `max_of(numbers)` already has one test using `[1, 2, 3]`. Which added tests would cover new situations? Select all that apply.
rubric: Negatives, a single element and an empty list are distinct cases.
Other increasing lists repeat what `[1, 2, 3]` already covers.

items.prompt: A suite has `test_create_user` and `test_delete_user`. The delete test looks up a user that the create test added. Run alone, `test_delete_user` fails, and after a random reorder it fails too. What change fixes the root problem?

options.label: Rename the tests so the create test always runs before delete
Retry the delete test three times until it finally passes
Let the delete test create its own user in its setup step
Add a sleep before delete so the user has time to be saved

rubric: Each test should arrange its own data so it is independent of order.
Renaming, sleeping and retrying keep the hidden dependency in place.

items.prompt: A function `is_eligible(age)` returns True for ages 18 to 65 inclusive. Which set of test inputs best checks its boundaries?
rubric: Boundary testing puts inputs on and just outside each edge: 17/18 and 65/66.
18, 40, 65 misses the outside values, so it cannot catch a wrong comparison operator.

items.prompt: `send_welcome(user, mailer)` calls `mailer.send(user.email, text)`. Which unit test checks this behaviour without sending real email?

options.label: Patch `send_welcome` to return True and assert that it returned True
Pass `None` as the mailer and assert that no exception is raised by the call
Pass a real SMTP mailer aimed at a personal inbox and check it by hand
Pass a fake mailer that records calls and assert it got the address once

rubric: A recording test double lets the test verify the interaction deterministically and in isolation.
Patching the function under test, or passing None, verifies nothing about the email being sent.

items.prompt: `apply_discount(19.99, 15)` returns a float of about 16.9915. Which assertion is the most reliable?

options.label: `assert apply_discount(19.99, 15) > 16`
`assert apply_discount(19.99, 15) == pytest.approx(16.9915)`
`assert apply_discount(19.99, 15) == 16.9915`
`assert str(apply_discount(19.99, 15)) == '16.9915'`

rubric: Floating-point results should be compared with a tolerance such as approx.
Exact equality and string comparison are fragile, and a loose > check would let wrong values pass.

items.prompt: Which pytest decorator runs `test_square(n, expected)` for the pairs (2, 4), (3, 9) and (-3, 9)?

options.label: `@pytest.mark.parametrize(['n', 'expected'], 2, 4, 3, 9, -3, 9)`
`@pytest.mark.parametrize('n, expected', [(2, 4), (3, 9)], [(-3, 9)])`
`@pytest.mark.parametrize('n, expected', [2, 3, -3], [4, 9, 9])`
`@pytest.mark.parametrize('n, expected', [(2, 4), (3, 9), (-3, 9)])`

rubric: Parametrize takes a comma-separated names string and one list of tuples, one tuple per case.
The other forms split names or values into the wrong argument shapes.

items.prompt: You add a pure function `income_tax(amount)` with 12 tax brackets and no external dependencies. Which test approach fits best?

options.label: A manual spreadsheet check done by hand before each release
A table of unit tests covering each bracket and its edges
An integration test that boots the database and web server
One end-to-end browser test that submits a checkout form

rubric: A pure, branchy function is best covered by fast, table-driven unit tests at the bracket boundaries.
End-to-end and integration tests are slow and indirect for this, and manual checks are not automated.

items.prompt: A function `token()` builds its result from the current time and a random salt, so its tests fail at random. Which changes make the tests deterministic? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add `sleep(1)` before asserting
Seed the random generator or inject the salt
Run the test three times and take the majority result
Inject a fixed clock function in the test

rubric: Controlling time and randomness removes the nondeterminism at its source.
Sleeping or voting over reruns only hides flakiness without fixing it.

items.prompt: A function runs `if a > 0: f1()` and then, independently, `if b > 0: f2()`. There are no else branches. Your team requires 100% branch coverage of this function. What is the minimum number of test cases needed?
rubric: One test with a>0 and b>0 takes both true branches; one with both non-positive takes both false branches.
Four would be needed for all combinations, but branch coverage does not require that.

items.prompt: A test passes when run alone but fails in the full suite, and only after `test_create_user` has run earlier. Both tests use the same database. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The database is slow under load, so every test needs a longer timeout
Left-over rows from the earlier test change the state this test expects
The test runner skips some assertions when many tests run together
The failing test has too few assertions to be reliable in a suite

rubric: Order-dependent failures point to shared state that one test leaves behind for another.
Timeouts and assertion counts do not explain why the failure depends on a specific earlier test.

items.prompt: A test for `calculate_total(cart)` only asserts `result is not None`. A change makes the total double, and every test still passes. What is the flaw?

options.label: The test should run end to end, since unit tests cannot verify numeric values
The function needs more mocks so that the total can be verified indirectly through calls
The assertion checks existence, not the computed value, so wrong totals pass
The coverage figure was too low, so the bug could not have been found

rubric: A weak assertion lets wrong output through; the test must check the expected total.
Unit tests can verify values, and coverage measures execution, not the strength of assertions.

items.prompt: Unit tests mock `PaymentClient.charge` to return `{'ok': True}`. The real API returns `{'status': 'ok'}`, so checkout breaks in production while all tests pass. What is the root cause?

options.label: The tests lack enough assertions about how often the mock is called
Mocks should never stand in for external services, so every test must call the real API
The mock's shape drifted from the real contract and nothing checks them
The checkout code needs higher line coverage in its unit tests

rubric: A mock that disagrees with the real contract gives false confidence; a contract or integration test would catch the drift.
Call counts and line coverage would not reveal a wrong response shape.

items.prompt: A repository method builds a SQL query with a JOIN on the wrong column. Unit tests using a mocked database connection all pass. Which test would most directly expose the bug?

options.label: An integration test running the query against a real test database
A unit test with a stricter mock that asserts the exact SQL string was sent
A linter rule that checks the SQL string for syntax mistakes only
A snapshot test of HTTP responses with the repository stubbed out

rubric: Only running the query against a real database shows whether it returns the right rows.
String assertions, stubbed layers and syntax linting cannot detect a logically wrong join.

items.prompt: A module reports 95% line coverage, yet a bug in its discount logic ships. The tests call `price()` along every discount path. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: Line coverage above 90% guarantees that all branches are verified
The module should have been tested only through end-to-end flows
Tests executed the lines but never asserted on the discount results
Coverage tools miss bugs only in code that has no conditionals

rubric: Coverage shows code ran, not that its output was checked; missing assertions let the bug through.
High line coverage does not guarantee branch coverage or correct results.

items.prompt: An end-to-end checkout test fails intermittently in CI but passes locally. Which are likely causes worth investigating? Select all that apply.

options.label: Several tests sharing one user account and its cart state
Dependence on a live third-party sandbox that is sometimes slow
Writing assertions after the final page action
Using descriptive names for test functions
Fixed `sleep(2)` waits instead of waiting for a condition

rubric: Timing assumptions, shared state and external dependencies are classic sources of end-to-end flakiness.
Test naming does not affect pass/fail behaviour, and asserting after the last action is normal.

items.prompt: After a refactor split `OrderService.place()` into two private helpers, 14 unit tests fail although behaviour is unchanged. The tests use mocks and assert that `helper_a` was called once before `helper_b`. What does this analysis show?

options.label: The refactor changed behaviour in a way the tests rightly caught
The tests are coupled to implementation steps rather than observable behaviour
The tests are fine, and refactoring should wait until coverage hits 100%
The suite needs more mocks so that each helper can be verified in isolation first

rubric: Tests asserting internal call order break on behaviour-preserving refactors; they should assert outcomes.
Adding more mocks would deepen the coupling, and the failures do not signal a behaviour change.

items.prompt: A test passes when run alone but fails when the whole suite runs in random order. Which is the most likely root cause?

options.label: The assertion library compares values differently once many test files are loaded together
The runner skips setup hooks whenever tests are shuffled, so fixtures are never created at all
Another test leaves modified global state that this test relies on or collides with
The test is so small that it cannot be executed reliably next to other fast tests

rubric: Order-dependent failures typically come from shared mutable state leaking between tests.
Distractors blame tooling or test size, which rarely explains order-dependent failures.

items.prompt: Unit tests for OrderService mock PaymentClient to return {status: 'ok'} and all pass. In production orders fail because the real client returns {state: 'OK'}. What does this best indicate?

options.label: Mocking is invalid for any collaborator that crosses a network boundary, so real calls are needed everywhere
The tests needed more assertions on the values that OrderService returns to its own callers
The mock encoded an assumed contract that drifted from the real client, and nothing checks that contract
Line coverage of OrderService was too low to catch a mismatch in the response shape

rubric: The mock's assumed response diverged from the real client; a contract or integration check would catch it.
Other options blame coverage or ban mocking rather than diagnosing contract drift.

items.prompt: A suite has 100% line coverage, yet a mutation tool reports that changing `>=` to `>` in a discount rule survives. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Tests run the line but never assert on the boundary value, so the changed behavior goes unnoticed
The mutation tool is wrong, because a fully covered line cannot contain a surviving mutant
Unit tests cannot observe comparison operators, so only an integration test could detect this
Branch coverage was disabled, so the tool miscounted which lines had actually been executed

rubric: Executing a line is not the same as asserting its behavior; no boundary-value assertion lets the mutant survive.
Distractors deny the mutant or blame tooling and test level.

items.prompt: A CI suite of 300 integration tests takes 40 minutes. Profiling shows each test rebuilds the database schema through migrations, about 7 seconds apiece. Which change targets the actual cause?

options.label: Mock the database driver in every test so that no schema needs to exist at all
Run migrations once per run and isolate tests using transaction rollback or table truncation
Run the tests in parallel against one shared database without any cleanup between them
Replace the integration tests with browser end-to-end tests that cover more behavior per run

rubric: The cost is repeated schema setup; set it up once and isolate data cheaply.
Other options change the test's nature or introduce shared-state problems.

items.prompt: A test asserting that a token expires 30 minutes after issue fails only on CI runs between 23:45 and 00:15 UTC. Which cause best fits?

options.label: The test uses so many mocks that they expire after a fixed time window has elapsed on CI
The test reads the real clock and compares calendar dates, so crossing midnight changes the outcome
Randomly generated token values occasionally collide during that particular window of the night
CI machines have less memory at that hour, causing token generation to time out intermittently

rubric: Failures tied to a time window point to an unfrozen clock and date-boundary logic.
Distractors invent resource or randomness causes that don't explain the midnight pattern.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest tests are coupled to implementation details rather than to behavior? Select all that apply.

options.label: Changing an internal data structure forces edits to many unrelated assertions
Renaming a private helper method breaks several tests that never call it directly
Tests verify the exact order of internal calls made on mock collaborators
A test fails when the function returns a wrong value for valid public input
Tests supply public API inputs and assert only on the returned outputs

rubric: Breakage from private renames, call-order checks and internal structure changes signals coupling to implementation.
Failing on a wrong public output, or asserting only on outputs, is behavior-focused.

items.prompt: A developer extracts a method and renames an internal class without changing behavior. Forty tests fail, all of which use mocks with `verify(...)` calls on internal collaborators. What is the most accurate analysis?

options.label: Mocks always make tests brittle, so every mock should be replaced by state-based assertions
The refactor silently changed behavior, and the failing tests have correctly caught the regression
The suite lacks end-to-end tests, which would have absorbed the internal change without failing
The tests assert on interactions with internals, so they encode structure rather than observable behavior

rubric: Interaction verification on internals ties tests to structure, so behavior-preserving refactors break them.
Other options assume a behavior change or overgeneralize against all mocks.

items.prompt: A pure tax function has 12 income brackets with boundary rules. Criteria: cover every bracket edge, run in under a second in CI, and pinpoint failures precisely. Which approach is best?

options.label: Browser end-to-end tests that enter each income through the UI and read the displayed tax
Parametrized unit tests on the function using values at and around each bracket edge
Integration tests through the HTTP API against a seeded database for every bracket edge
Manual exploratory testing before each release, with results recorded in a shared spreadsheet

rubric: Pure logic with many boundaries suits fast, precise parametrized unit tests.
Higher-level or manual options are slower and localize failures poorly.

items.prompt: A manager mandates 90% line coverage as a merge gate. Which critique is the most sound?

options.label: Ninety percent is too low, because full line coverage is what ensures the covered code has few defects
It invites tests that run code without assertions, so it measures execution, not verification
Line coverage is a poor proxy for quality, so the team should track branch coverage in its place and gate on that
Coverage gates suit integration tests better, because unit tests exercise too few lines to reach any threshold

rubric: A coverage target used as a gate rewards running code, not checking it, so assertion-free tests can satisfy it.
Distractors overreact, overpromise on 100%, or invent a level restriction.

items.prompt: A repository layer uses raw SQL with JSON operators and unique-constraint handling. Criteria: catch dialect and constraint errors, and keep the suite under 5 minutes. Which approach is best?

options.label: An in-memory fake repository backed by dictionaries, used for every query test in the suite
An embedded database of a different engine that claims to emulate most production syntax
Tests against the production engine in a throwaway container with a few seeded rows per test
Mock the database driver and assert that each generated SQL string equals the expected query text

rubric: Only the real engine reveals dialect and constraint behavior, and containers with small data stay fast.
Fakes, string-matching mocks and different engines miss real SQL behavior.

items.prompt: A test fails in about 3% of runs and blocks merges. Criteria: keep the pipeline unblocked, don't lose the signal, and ensure the root cause is fixed. Which handling is best?

options.label: Add automatic retries to the whole suite until it passes, and leave the cause unexamined
Delete the test because it gives no reliable signal, and plan to rewrite it at some point
Quarantine it into a non-blocking run with an owner and deadline, then fix the root cause
Keep it blocking so the pain forces someone to fix it, with no change to the pipeline

rubric: Quarantine with ownership unblocks merges while retaining visibility and a fix commitment.
Blanket retries, deletion or doing nothing fail one or more criteria.

items.prompt: For a checkout app, criteria: confidence that the purchase journey works across payment, inventory and UI, low maintenance cost, and fast feedback. Which test distribution is best?

options.label: Many unit tests for logic, some integration tests for services, a few E2E tests on key purchase paths
Mostly end-to-end tests covering each rule and branch, so scenarios run as users would see them and catch UI, payment and inventory defects together
Mostly unit tests with collaborators mocked, plus a manual check before release, since unit tests are the fastest to run and cheapest to maintain
A roughly equal number of tests at each level, to balance speed against realism in equal parts and avoid over-relying on one kind

rubric: A pyramid-shaped mix gives fast feedback and cheap upkeep while still checking the key journey end to end.
Other options are slow and costly, miss integration risk, or ignore cost per level.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to delete an existing automated test? Select all that apply.

options.label: It verifies behavior that was intentionally removed from the product
It is slow, so it is inconvenient to run on a developer's laptop
It duplicates another test's assertions exactly, at the same level and with the same setup
It fails occasionally, so it must be wrong and has no value

rubric: Tests of removed behavior and exact duplicates add cost with no protection.
Slowness or flakiness calls for fixing or moving the test, not automatic deletion.

items.prompt: You must change a 300-line pricing function that has no tests, due next week. Its behavior is not fully documented. Criteria: avoid regressions, limited time, and unknown current rules. What is the best first step?

options.label: Make the change, then rely on the QA team's manual regression pass scheduled for the days just before the release
Write characterization tests pinning current outputs for sample inputs, then change the code
Rewrite the function cleanly first with a simpler design, then write tests against the new code once it is done
Write unit tests from the product spec alone, ignoring what the current code outputs, and fix any code that fails them

rubric: Characterization tests capture actual behavior cheaply, giving a regression net before the change.
Rewriting first, late manual QA, or spec-only tests leave current behavior unprotected.

items.prompt: A team says its suite is strong because line coverage is 95%. A mutation run shows only 55% of injected mutants are killed. Which conclusion is best supported by these two numbers?

options.label: Many executed lines have no assertions that would detect a behaviour change, so coverage overstates fault-detection power.
The suite is adequate, because the surviving mutants are almost certainly equivalent mutants that cannot change behaviour.
Branch coverage would have shown the same 55% figure, so switching coverage metric would expose the weakness exactly.
The mutation tool is miscalibrated, since coverage above 90% guarantees that most injected faults will be caught.

rubric: Coverage measures execution, not verification; surviving mutants show missing or weak assertions.
Distractors assume coverage implies detection or dismiss survivors wholesale as equivalent.

items.prompt: An integration test fails about 3% of runs because it asserts right after an async event whose timing varies. Criteria: keep the failure signal trustworthy, don't hide real race bugs, keep CI moving. Which response is best?

options.label: Delete the test, since a nondeterministic test gives no reliable information and slows every pipeline run it appears in.
Configure CI to retry the test up to three times so intermittent failures no longer appear in the reports.
Reproduce the race, wait on the event condition, and quarantine the test meanwhile with an owner and deadline.
Increase the fixed sleep before the assertion to five seconds so the event always completes before it is checked.

rubric: Condition-based waiting removes the nondeterminism and temporary tracked quarantine protects the signal.
Retries and longer sleeps mask the problem; deletion discards coverage of a real behaviour.

items.prompt: A repository class is unit-tested with a mocked DB driver; each test asserts the exact SQL string passed to `execute`. The team wants tests that survive refactors yet catch wrong queries. How should the approach be judged?

options.label: Flawed only because mocks are slow; replacing them with stubs returning canned rows would fix the weakness.
Brittle: it couples tests to query text and cannot show the query is correct; run against a real lightweight database.
Sound, provided every mock is also verified to be called exactly once so interaction coverage is complete.
Sound, because asserting exact SQL isolates the unit completely and keeps the tests fast and fully deterministic.

rubric: Verifying SQL text tests implementation, not behaviour, and passes even when the query returns wrong data.
Distractors treat isolation or call counts as evidence of correctness.

items.prompt: Twelve teams own microservices deployed independently. The 90-minute E2E suite is the only check, and breaking API changes are still found late. Criteria: fast feedback, independent deploys, catching interface breakage. Which strategy is best?

options.label: Run consumer-driven contract tests in each service's pipeline, plus a small E2E smoke suite for critical journeys.
Have each team mock its neighbouring services in unit tests written from the current API docs, so interface mismatches show up early in each pipeline.
Add E2E scenarios for each pair of services and run them on every commit, since full-system runs exercise the real interfaces most faithfully.
Hold deployments until the E2E suite passes for all services together, so the exact combination of versions is tested before release.

rubric: Contract tests verify interface compatibility quickly and independently; a thin E2E layer covers wiring.
Other options slow feedback, couple deploys, or rely on mocks that drift from reality.

items.prompt: For a payments codebase, leadership proposes policies for coverage. Criteria: discourage assertion-free tests, focus effort on risky logic, keep the metric useful. Which policy is best?

options.label: Require 100% line coverage on the payment and ledger modules at merge, so that risky code is exercised by tests before release.
Review coverage gaps on high-risk modules, add mutation checks there, and treat the number as a signal, not a target.
Set an 80% project-wide threshold, fail any commit that lowers the total, and review the exceptions in each quarterly audit.
Stop tracking coverage and rely on code review and manual exploratory testing, since numeric targets tend to get gamed.

rubric: Risk-focused use plus mutation checks addresses assertion-free tests while keeping coverage informative.
Distractors either make the metric a target (Goodhart) or discard useful information.

items.prompt: A team uses large snapshot tests of rendered output for a complex UI. Which are valid criticisms of this practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Incidental changes cause noisy failures, which trains developers to regenerate snapshots without reading diffs.
Large snapshots are often approved without careful review, so unintended changes get accepted unnoticed.
Snapshot tests cannot run in CI because storing snapshots requires an interactive browser session.
Snapshots assert on intended behaviour rather than raw output, so they never fail when a regression occurs.

rubric: Review fatigue and noisy failures are the real weaknesses of broad snapshots.
The other options invent technical limits or reverse what snapshots assert.

items.prompt: A team's suite is 70% UI-driven E2E tests taking 40 minutes, with 8% flaky failures and few unit tests. Developers now ignore red builds. The goal is fast, trusted feedback on each pull request without losing coverage of critical user journeys. What should the team do first?

options.label: Rewrite every E2E test in a newer browser automation tool, since the flakiness comes mainly from the current framework.
Push logic checks down into unit and integration tests, keep a few stable E2E journeys, and fix or quarantine the flaky ones.
Run the whole E2E suite on more machines in parallel so the existing tests finish faster while remaining unchanged.
Make red builds block merges strictly, so developers are forced to investigate every failure regardless of cause.

rubric: Rebalancing toward cheaper, deterministic tests and stabilising a thin E2E layer restores trust and speed.
Distractors speed up or enforce a bad suite instead of fixing its shape.

items.prompt: A function `is_valid(token, now)` is replaced by `is_valid(token)` that reads the system clock; tokens expire after exactly 30 minutes. Design the test that is deterministic and covers the boundary. Which design meets both needs?

options.label: Set expiry to one second in test config, sleep 1.1 seconds, and assert the token is rejected afterwards.
Assert only that a freshly issued token is valid and an obviously old, hard-coded token is rejected.
Create a token, sleep 30 minutes in the test, then assert it is invalid to exercise real elapsed time.
Inject a controllable clock and assert validity at 29:59, 30:00 and 30:01 after issuance, per the stated rule.

rubric: An injected clock removes real waiting and lets the test probe the exact boundary.
Sleeping is slow or flaky, and skipping boundary values leaves the edge untested.

items.prompt: A payment API must be idempotent: clients retry with the same idempotency key after timeouts, sometimes concurrently. Which test design best verifies that a customer is never charged twice?

options.label: Send the same request twice in sequence and assert both responses return HTTP 200 with identical, well-formed JSON bodies.
Mock the gateway and assert it was called exactly once after a single request, then confirm the response matches the happy path.
Unit-test the idempotency key generator to confirm it returns unique values across a million generated calls without any collision.
Use a fake gateway counting charges; replay one key sequentially and concurrently, asserting one charge and identical responses.

rubric: Observing the side effect count under sequential and concurrent replays tests the actual guarantee.
Other designs check the wrong property or ignore concurrency.

items.prompt: You must specify property-based tests for `merge_sorted(a, b)`, which merges two sorted lists, so that almost any wrong implementation fails. Which set of properties is sufficient?

options.label: Output is sorted and has the same length as the two inputs combined, for generated sorted inputs.
Output is sorted, and its elements form the same multiset as `a + b`, for generated sorted inputs.
Output equals the expected result for five hand-picked pairs, including empty lists and duplicate values.
Output contains every element of `a`, and its length equals `len(a) + len(b)`, for generated inputs.

rubric: Sortedness plus multiset equality fully determines the output.
Length-only checks let wrong elements through, and fixed examples are not generative.

items.prompt: Integration tests share one database and now run in 8 parallel workers, causing random failures from leaked rows. Constraints: keep the parallelism, keep tests realistic, no ordering dependencies. Which fix meets all of them?

options.label: Insert short sleeps between tests so each worker's writes finish before another worker begins reading from the shared tables.
Give each worker its own schema or rolled-back transaction, and create unique data via factories per test.
Run the integration tests serially again, which removes all the interference at the cost of much longer total runtime.
Add a fixed ordering to the tests so rows created by one test are cleaned up by the test that runs right after it.

rubric: Isolation per worker with unique data keeps realism and parallelism without coupling tests.
Serial runs lose parallelism; ordering and sleeps create hidden dependencies.

items.prompt: A 6,000-line legacy module with no tests and unclear specs must be refactored safely this quarter. Which plan best creates a safety net before any changes are made?

options.label: Write tests from the outdated design document and fix every failure first, so the code's behaviour matches the documented intent before refactoring begins.
Rewrite the module from scratch against a fresh specification, then compare the old and new versions' behaviour informally on a few sample runs.
Record current outputs on representative and edge inputs as characterization tests, then refactor in small steps keeping them green.
Add unit tests only for new code written during the refactor, and have two reviewers read the old code carefully line by line for defects.

rubric: Characterization tests pin existing behaviour so refactoring changes can be detected.
Other plans test intended rather than actual behaviour or provide no net for old code.

items.prompt: You must plan tests for a new third-party payment integration. Constraints: CI never calls the real provider, provider API changes must be detected, and your error handling must be verified. Which elements belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: A nightly run charging real cards in production to confirm the integration behaves as in the sandbox.
A scheduled contract test against the provider's sandbox that flags changes to response formats or fields.
Mocks of every internal class that touches the integration, so each class is tested in complete isolation.
A fake provider server replaying recorded responses, including timeouts and declines, to exercise your error handling in CI.

rubric: A fake covers error paths offline, and sandbox contract checks detect provider drift.
Mocking all internals adds brittleness; production charges violate the no-real-calls constraint.

items.prompt: A pipeline takes 45 minutes per pull request: 5 minutes of unit tests, 15 of integration tests, 25 of E2E. Goal: PR feedback under 10 minutes, with integration and E2E coverage still enforced before release. Which pipeline design meets both constraints?

options.label: Delete the integration tests that take longest and rely on unit tests plus a manual QA pass before every release.
On PRs run unit and impacted integration tests in shards; run full integration and E2E on merge, gating release.
Tag slow tests to be skipped permanently on all branches, then re-enable them only if production incidents reveal gaps.
Run everything on one larger machine with longer timeouts so the same tests complete a bit faster overall.

rubric: Tiered, sharded PR checks give fast feedback while full suites still gate release.
Other options drop coverage, barely change speed, or defer detection to production.
